headline: Lisa Carter-Bawa: Oncology nurses should lead with empathy, not smoking history
dek: Carter-Bawa told Oncology Nursing News that nurses can reduce blame in lung cancer care, take part in research and press for coverage of follow-up scans after screening.
body:
Oncology nurses can reduce blame by leading with empathy rather than smoking history, according to Lisa Carter-Bawa, PhD, MPH, APRN, ANP-C, FAAN, FSBM. She is director of the Cancer Prevention Precision Control Institute at the Hackensack Meridian Center for Discovery and Innovation and deputy associate director for community outreach and engagement at Georgetown Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. She spoke in an October 2026 interview with Oncology Nursing News.

Carter-Bawa acknowledged that smoking history matters clinically for treatment options, but said that opening with the question is "blameful and it shuts patients down". She recommended asking first how the person is doing and what they need right now. When smoking history is needed, she said, nurses should explain why it is being asked and how it could affect treatment.

She also encouraged nurses to see everyday problems as research questions. Frustrations with workflows or how regimens are given, she noted, can become quality improvement projects. She urged nurses to engage when researchers visit their units, saying many are looking for clinical partners to help ground their work in questions that matter.

On policy, Carter-Bawa said that because the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends lung cancer screening, the scan itself is covered, but follow-up scans may not be. "We should really cover the entire continuum because that could be a barrier to someone getting scanned," she said.

Oncology Nursing News cited a study of 6268 commercially insured adults who underwent low-dose CT screening. Of these, 7.4% had a downstream procedure within 12 months, and some faced out-of-pocket costs for that care.

Carter-Bawa said stigma reduction, early detection and precision treatment are "now going in the same direction", creating "a potentially synergistic moment in time".
key_quote: The oncology nurse that’s at the bedside, their everyday issues are research questions just waiting to be tested

source.title: Don't Lead With 'Did You Smoke?': Lung Cancer Advice for Oncology Nurses

extra.scout_summary: Lung screening researcher Lisa Carter-Bawa discusses how AI could flag patients eligible for low-dose CT lung cancer screening while nurses remain the human in the loop. The article also covers non-stigmatising ways to ask about smoking history and cost barriers to follow-up after screening.
